transcript: I definitely don't wanna spoil the fun around this star-studded production of Twelfth Night Shakespeare in the park is a fun time the tickets are free it's great to be back in the newly renovated Delacorte Theatre in these new plastic seats that are marginally more comfortable than the old metal ones and of course it's fun to see all these big stars together on stage there's a lot to enjoy about it I definitely wouldn't deter anyone from going especially if it's your first Shakespeare in the Park the event as a whole is great but as a production of Twelfth Night it didn't totally land for me before the show I was talking to my friend about what we think makes for a good rendition of Twelfth Night and I was saying that obviously Twelfth Night is one of Shakespeare's funniest comedies but it also has these undertones of melancholy to it I've seen some productions of Twelfth Night that were actually very somber at times And every director kinda has to decide how much to lean into that or not and funny enough I said to my friend that I usually prefer it when they *don't* lean into it when they just let it be light and funny and then the audience can make of the darker undertones what they will so ironically even after having that whole conversation I watched this very lighthearted production of Twelfth Night and I couldn't shake the feeling that specific cast would have absolutely kiIIed it in a more serious production of Twelfth Night I look at Lupita Nyong’o and Peter Dinklage in particular both heavyweights in the world of dramatic acting and both playing characters here that are kind of at the emotional core of their respective plot threads and I felt like both of them were trying really hard to be funny and they kind of were but I just don't think it was their strong suit It reminded me of like when your school principal cracked a joke that one time and it was fun to see that side of them but they didn't make you laugh the way that the actually funny teachers did it wasn't just them though I felt like everyone in this production was working really hard to come up with the next bit, the next gag and with Shakespeare comedy I do think you have to make it your own so I appreciate the strong choices here and some of them worked for me like probably my favorite thing about this production was Duke Orsino in this version he's like a high-end fitness bro with this whole entourage of hype men wearing suits like it was so funny and original but it also felt like an organic extension of the world we were in and it even tells us something about Orsino and how he relates to power and ego but a lot of the other stuff felt very forced to me and maybe part of it was just that it wasn't to my sense of humor but I also don't think there was much in the way of comedic vision here there was a charming sense of playfulness but it wore off kinda quickly for me because it felt scattered and unfocused I almost got the sense that they were more focused on engineering the most splashy widely appealing event that they possibly could to reopen the Delacorte then they were on actually telling the story of Twelfth Night and the first part of that is great but I don't think they had to be mutually exclusive in fact this is the same director as Merry Wives which reopened the Delacorte after the theater shut downs and it's a great counter example of how you can find widely appealing accessible comedy through a very specific vision
